title: Direct laryngoscopy and microlaryngoscopy with biopsy
subtitle: Agree the airway first, map before you bite

sources.org: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
sources.title: Cancer of the upper aerodigestive tract: assessment and management in people aged 16 and over (NG36)

sources.org: ENT UK and partner specialty associations (UK National Multidisciplinary Guidelines)
sources.title: Laryngeal cancer: United Kingdom National Multidisciplinary Guidelines (Jones TM et al., J Laryngol Otol)
Difficult Airway Society 2015 guidelines for management of unanticipated difficult intubation in adults

indications: Histological diagnosis and staging of a suspected laryngeal, hypopharyngeal or oropharyngeal cancer seen on flexible nasendoscopy, with assessment of extent for the MDT.
Excision biopsy or treatment of benign vocal fold lesions (polyps, cysts, nodules not responding to voice therapy, papillomatosis) and of leukoplakia or suspected dysplasia.
Assessment of airway stenosis, persistent unexplained hoarseness or a lesion that cannot be fully seen in clinic.
Search for a primary in a patient with a metastatic neck node and unknown primary, as part of panendoscopy with targeted biopsies.
contraindications: An obstructing airway lesion where general anaesthesia without a secured airway is unsafe. The airway plan comes first, which may mean awake tracheostomy or awake fibreoptic intubation before the biopsy.
Severe cervical spine disease or instability that prevents the neck position needed for exposure; consider flexible endoscopic biopsy under local anaesthesia.
Uncorrected coagulopathy for biopsy of a vascular lesion.
Where imaging is still needed for staging, scan before the biopsy where possible, because biopsy oedema can distort the images.
preparation: Review the flexible nasendoscopy images or video with the anaesthetist: the size and site of the lesion, its effect on the airway, and the expected difficulty of exposure.
Cross-sectional imaging for suspected malignancy, ideally before biopsy, as set out in the UK laryngeal cancer guideline.
Agree the ventilation technique: small-bore microlaryngoscopy tube, jet ventilation, or tubeless techniques; and laser safety precautions if a laser will be used.

Consent risks to discuss: damage to teeth, lips, gums and tongue; sore throat; change in voice, which may be permanent after vocal fold surgery; bleeding; airway swelling and the rare need for a tracheostomy; tongue numbness or taste change from pressure; perforation of the pharynx or oesophagus if the oesophagus is examined; and that the biopsy may be non-diagnostic and need repeating.
positioning: Supine with the neck flexed on the chest and the head extended at the atlanto-occipital joint (the sniffing position), on a head ring with a pillow or adjustable headrest.
Table height so the surgeon looks down the laryngoscope with a straight back; the suspension frame rests on a chest support or a Mayo table, never on the chest wall alone.
Eyes taped and protected from instruments and from laser if used.
equipment: Range of operating laryngoscopes, including an anterior commissure laryngoscope, and suspension apparatus.
Operating microscope with a long focal length objective lens suitable for laryngeal work, and 0, 30 and 70 degree rigid endoscopes with camera and recording.
Microlaryngeal instruments: cupped and straight biting forceps, microscissors, sickle knife, fine suction; topical adrenaline on counted neurosurgical patties with strings.
Tooth guard; rigid oesophagoscope or pharyngoscope if panendoscopy is planned; laser with laser-safe tube, wet patties and fire precautions if planned.
anatomy: The larynx has three subsites: the supraglottis (epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds, false cords, ventricles), the glottis (true vocal folds and the anterior and posterior commissures), and the subglottis down to the lower border of the cricoid.

The vocal fold is layered: epithelium, the superficial lamina propria (Reinke's space), the vocal ligament and the vocalis muscle. Voice quality depends on the superficial lamina propria being preserved.
The anterior commissure is where the two folds meet. Raw surfaces on both sides here heal with a web.
The hypopharynx comprises the piriform fossae, the posterior pharyngeal wall and the postcricoid region; a systematic examination includes them for any cancer workup.
The vallecula and tongue base sit above the epiglottis, and are examined and palpated for the unknown primary and for supraglottic extension.
criticalSafety: The airway plan is agreed before induction, including what happens if the lesion bleeds or swells after biopsy and the patient cannot be extubated.
Protect the upper teeth; never lever on them to gain exposure.
Map and photograph the lesion before biopsy; biopsy changes the appearance and the next person cannot see what you saw.
Count patties in and out; a patty left in the larynx or trachea obstructs the airway.
For benign vocal fold lesions, preserve the superficial lamina propria and avoid raw surfaces at both sides of the anterior commissure.
structuresAtRisk: Vocal fold layered structure and the anterior commissure
Lingual and hypoglossal nerves (pressure from the laryngoscope)
Pharyngeal and oesophageal wall if rigid oesophagoscopy is performed
commonErrors: Taking a small superficial biopsy from the necrotic centre of a tumour, which returns as non-diagnostic.
Failing to examine the subglottis, ventricles and hypopharynx, so the stage is wrong.
Stripping the whole vocal fold mucosa for a benign or dysplastic lesion.
Not recording the exposure difficulty and the airway findings for the anaesthetist who will see the patient next.
complications: Dental injury, lip and tongue injury, tongue numbness or taste change from pressure.
Airway oedema or bleeding after biopsy, occasionally needing reintubation or tracheostomy; laryngospasm at extubation.
Voice change, vocal fold scarring or anterior commissure web.
Pharyngeal or oesophageal perforation after rigid endoscopy, presenting with pain, fever, surgical emphysema or tachycardia.
postop: Observe for stridor and bleeding. Humidified oxygen and a plan agreed with the anaesthetist for patients with a bulky airway lesion; some need high-dependency care.
Voice rest according to the surgeon's instruction for vocal fold surgery, and voice therapy referral where indicated.
If the oesophagus was examined with a rigid scope, check for chest or neck pain, fever and surgical emphysema before oral intake.
Results go to the head and neck MDT; give the patient a date and a named contact for the results.

steps.emphasis: Teeth, voice change and the airway risks discussed. For suspected cancer, the patient knows this is a diagnostic operation and when results are expected.
Flexible nasendoscopy images and the imaging on screen. Agree the subsites to examine and biopsy.
No routine antibiotics. VTE assessment. The anaesthetist may give dexamethasone to reduce airway oedema.

Microlaryngoscopy tube, jet ventilation or tubeless technique agreed; laser fire precautions if a laser is used. For an obstructing lesion, the surgeon is scrubbed at induction with the tracheostomy set open.
Sniffing position. Chest support for the suspension arm placed before the laryngoscope goes in.
Long focal length objective so the microscope works down the laryngoscope; leave room for instruments.
Adrenaline-soaked patties on strings, pressure, and suction diathermy for discrete points. Reinspect after the patties come out.
Every patty and the tooth guard accounted for; the larynx and hypopharynx free of clot before extubation.
Patties counted out by number and checked against the strings.
Each biopsy site in a separate, labelled pot with the subsite named; state the clinical question on the form.
State the lesion, the bleeding and swelling risk, and the plan if stridor develops.
Draw or describe the lesion map by subsite, attach the photographs, and record exposure difficulty and the laryngoscope that worked.

step.mll.insert.title: Introduce the laryngoscope without using the teeth
step.mll.insert.why: Exposure of the larynx is achieved by lifting the tongue and hyoid forward along the laryngoscope's axis. Levering against the teeth breaks them and rarely improves the view.
how: Open the mouth with the fingers of the left hand, protecting the upper teeth and lips with the tooth guard.
Insert the laryngoscope along the right side of the tongue, moving the tongue to the left, and advance in the midline to see the epiglottis.
Lift the epiglottis with the tip and advance into the larynx, lifting along the line of the handle. Avoid catching the lips between the scope and the teeth.
If the view is poor, ask for external laryngeal pressure, change the head position, or choose a different laryngoscope before forcing the current one.
pitfalls: Pivoting on the upper incisors to gain an anterior view.
Displacing a small tube while manoeuvring the laryngoscope; watch the capnograph and tell the anaesthetist.

step.mll.survey.title: Systematic examination and lesion mapping before biopsy
step.mll.survey.why: The MDT stages the tumour from this examination. A lesion seen only in part, or an extension into the subglottis or hypopharynx that is missed, puts the patient into the wrong treatment.
how: Examine in a fixed order: oral cavity, tongue base and vallecula, epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds, false cords, ventricles, true cords, anterior and posterior commissures, subglottis, then piriform fossae, posterior pharyngeal wall and postcricoid region.
Use 0, 30 and 70 degree endoscopes to see the ventricles, the undersurface of the cords and the subglottis.
Palpate the tongue base and tonsils, and note vocal fold mobility as seen in clinic.
Photograph or record the lesion and its extent before biopsy, and state the subsites involved aloud.
pitfalls: Biopsying the first abnormality seen and stopping the examination.
Missing subglottic extension because only a zero degree view was used.

step.mll.suspend.title: Suspend the laryngoscope
step.mll.suspend.why: Suspension frees both hands for microsurgery and gives a stable view under the microscope. A suspension arm resting on the patient's chest compresses it and moves with every breath.
how: Attach the suspension arm to the laryngoscope and rest it on a chest support or a Mayo table, not the chest wall.
Adjust to bring the lesion into the centre of the view, using the minimum force needed.
Check again that the teeth and lips are free and that ventilation pressures are unchanged.
pitfalls: Excessive suspension force for a long time, causing tongue numbness and taste change.
Suspending with the lesion at the edge of the view, then working at an angle.

step.mll.biopsy.title: Biopsy: deep enough for diagnosis, conservative on the vocal fold
step.mll.biopsy.why: A suspected cancer needs tissue deep enough to show invasion, from the living edge of the tumour. A benign or premalignant vocal fold lesion needs the opposite: removal with the least possible disturbance of the layered fold, because the voice depends on it.
how: For a suspected cancer, take biopsies from the edge of the lesion where tumour meets normal mucosa, avoiding necrotic centres, and take enough tissue for diagnosis. Send separately any biopsy from a different subsite.

For a benign vocal fold lesion or leukoplakia, grasp the lesion with fine forceps, retract it medially and excise it with microscissors at its base, or raise a microflap, preserving the superficial lamina propria and the vocal ligament.
Avoid creating raw areas on both sides of the anterior commissure at the same operation.
Place an adrenaline patty on the biopsy site after each bite.
structuresAtRisk: Vocal ligament and superficial lamina propria
pitfalls: A superficial biopsy of a cancer that shows only dysplasia, leading to a repeat anaesthetic.
Stripping the whole fold for a small lesion, causing a stiff fold and a permanently poor voice.

step.mll.airway-bailout.title: Bail-out: failed exposure, bleeding or a threatened airway
step.mll.airway-bailout.why: The larynx is the airway. A bleeding biopsy site or a swollen tumour can turn a diagnostic procedure into an airway emergency, and repeated attempts at exposure cause the oedema that makes it worse.
how: Failed exposure: try a different laryngoscope, external counter-pressure and head repositioning. If still inadequate, stop and plan a flexible endoscopic biopsy or a different approach rather than forcing.
Bleeding: pressure with an adrenaline patty and suction diathermy, under vision, while the anaesthetist protects the airway. Do not extubate until it has stopped.

Airway compromise after biopsy of a bulky tumour: agree with the anaesthetist whether to keep the patient intubated and transfer to critical care, or to perform a tracheostomy before waking, according to the shared airway plan.
Inform the consultant and record the decision and its reasons.
pitfalls: Extubating a patient whose bulky lesion has just been biopsied without a plan for reintubation.
Repeated forceful laryngoscopy that causes swelling and bleeding.
